title: A filename with an embedded NUL byte sails through every path function, then blows up the moment you open it
assumption: If os.path.join / path.join didn't raise an error, the filename is safe to use.

input.display: "a\u0000b" (the letter a, a NUL byte, the letter b)
input.description: A filename decoded from untrusted bytes (a multipart upload, a binary protocol field) that was never validated as a 'reasonable' string before being treated as a filename.

what_goes_wrong: String-only path functions accept the NUL byte without complaint and happily build a joined path containing it; the error only appears later, at the actual filesystem call, in a different part of the codebase than where the bad input was first accepted.
why: os.path.join and path.join are pure string operations — they concatenate and, in Node's case, normalize separators, but neither inspects the byte content for anything the OS might reject. The OS filesystem call layer represents paths as NUL-terminated C strings, so an embedded NUL byte would truncate or corrupt the path at the syscall level; both Python's open() and Node's fs functions guard against this themselves and raise before making the call, rather than letting the OS ever see a truncated string.

repros.code:
import os.path
joined = os.path.join("a\x00b", "c")
print("join accepted it:", repr(joined))
try:
    open("a\x00b")
except ValueError as e:
    print("open() raised:", e)
repros.expected_output:
join accepted it: 'a\x00b/c'
open() raised: embedded null byte

join accepted it: "a\u0000b/c"
fs raised: ERR_INVALID_ARG_VALUE

fix: Validate filenames for control characters (including NUL) at the point you accept them, not at the point you happen to open them — the path-building layer in between will not catch it for you.

sources.title: Python docs: File Names, Command-Line Arguments, and Environment Variables

test_cases.note: Your file-open code should raise here, not silently truncate the filename at the NUL byte.
